data.text/markdown:
Write your own audience

A local explanation says why the model predicted this for this person. Who reads it changes what a good explanation is. A layperson needs words in place of log-odds. A data scientist wants the log-odds. A regulator wants the direction of every effect and no probability at all. EBaMl ships two audiences, Layperson and DataScientist, and the base class Audience lets you add your own. An audience does two jobs:
  1. It decides which facts the LLM gets. Seven methods (contribution, prediction, change, flip, class_output, margin and share) return the keys that the audience adds to one kind of fact. A number that the audience leaves out is a number that the LLM cannot repeat.
  2. It tells the LLM how to write. The method guidance returns the instruction, with its reason.
All eight methods are abstract, so an author decides on every model number. There are two ways in. Subclass a built-in audience and override the one method that differs: this is the short way. Subclass Audience and write all eight methods: this is the way for an audience with new rules. This notebook builds six audiences for six readers (a child, a chief executive, a reader of Simplified Technical English, a loan officer, a machine learning engineer and a regulator). It shows the facts that each one produces, and the errors you meet when an audience is wrong. To change only the language of the explanation, you need no audience: pass language= (see the languages notebook). Everything works without a key until the last cells. Those cells call the LLM, and they only run when you press their button. The default model needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY. To use another model, pass model=: see the documentation page "Choosing the model".

The model and the facts

The same Titanic EBM as in local_explanations.py: a binary classifier without interactions. The facts of one passenger come from compute_local_facts. No LLM is involved, and the facts do not depend on the audience.

data.text/markdown:
1. The short way: subclass a built-in audience

Some readers need the facts of a layperson (words, no model numbers) and a different instruction. For each of them, the class below subclasses Layperson and overrides guidance. The other seven methods stay as they are. The readers differ in role and style:
  • Eli5 is a child. The text uses short sentences and one everyday comparison.
  • Executive is a chief executive. The text opens with the bottom line and then gives the inputs that matter most.
  • SimplifiedEnglish is a reader of Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), for example a technician or a reader who learns English. The text uses one idea in each sentence and the same word for the same thing.
Each instruction gives the reason ("because a child follows an image better than a rule") as well as the order. A model follows a rule better when it knows the motive.

2. Change one rule: subclass DataScientist

Two readers start from the data scientist and change a rule. A machine learning engineer wants one more number for each input. A loan officer reads figures, but only one: the probability, as a percentage. The scores, the standard deviations and the confidence interval are noise for this reader. The class LoanOfficer subclasses DataScientist and overrides three methods:
  • contribution returns no key, so a contribution shows the feature and its value only.
  • prediction returns the probability as a percentage, in place of the probability, the interval and the logit.
  • guidance asks for percentages and no statistics.
The other methods keep the rules of the data scientist. The helper round_value rounds to the precision of the prompts. The machine learning engineer debugs the model. An effect that is small against its standard deviation can be noise from the training data. The class MLEngineer adds the key signal_to_noise (the size of the score divided by the standard deviation) to each contribution, and keeps every other rule of the data scientist.

3. New rules: subclass Audience

A regulator checks that the model uses the right inputs in the right direction. This reader wants the direction and the size of each effect, in words, and no probability at all, because a probability depends on the threshold of the bank. The class below subclasses Audience itself, so it writes all eight methods. Each one answers the question "which number does this reader get?". The answers are in the table:
Method Keys of this audience
contribution The direction and the size, in words, with the helpers points_towards and strength_word.
prediction None.
change The direction of the change of the score, in words.
flip Whether the flip holds under the uncertainty of the model.
class_output The likelihood of the class after the changes, in words.
margin None.
share A rough word, most or few, because the share is a sampling estimate.

The facts that each audience produces

facts_to_texts renders the same facts for each audience. Compare the tabs. Eli5, Executive and SimplifiedEnglish get the same facts as Layperson, because they only change guidance, so the tabs show Layperson for all four. The machine learning engineer gets signal_to_noise in addition to the data scientist's numbers. The loan officer gets percent. The regulator gets direction and size, and no probability. The LLM reads exactly these texts, so an audience that leaves a number out makes sure that the LLM never repeats it.

data.text/markdown:
The instruction of each audience

Layperson
The reader is not technical and knows no statistics, so write in everyday words. Express strength and likelihood in plain words such as 'strongly', 'slightly', 'very likely' or 'about as likely as not'. Mention only values of the person's own inputs (for example their age), because model numbers (scores, log-odds, probabilities, percentages, intervals, standard deviations) mean nothing to this reader.
Eli5
The reader is a child of about ten, so use short sentences, ordinary words and one comparison from everyday life, because a child follows an image better than a rule. Express strength and likelihood in plain words, and mention only values of the person's own inputs, because model numbers mean nothing to this reader.
Executive
The reader is a chief executive who has one minute, so open with the bottom line in one sentence. Then name the one or two inputs that matter most, because the reader decides on the result and not on the method. Use business words, and mention only values of the person's own inputs, because model numbers do not help this decision.
SimplifiedEnglish
The reader needs text with one meaning, so write in Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100): one idea in each sentence, at most 20 words in a sentence, the active voice, the simple present tense, and the same word for the same thing every time. Express strength and likelihood in plain words, and mention only values of the person's own inputs, because model numbers mean nothing to this reader.
DataScientist
The reader is a data scientist, so be precise. Quote the scores (log-odds contributions), probabilities and confidence intervals from the facts. Say how uncertain a statement is when the facts show wide confidence intervals.
MLEngineer
The reader is a machine learning engineer who debugs the model, so quote the score and the signal_to_noise of each input. Point out an input with a low signal_to_noise, because such an effect may be noise from the training data.
LoanOfficer
The reader is a loan officer who decides with percentages, so quote the percentage from the facts and skip the statistics of the model, because scores and intervals do not help the decision.
Regulator
The reader is a model regulator who checks the direction of every effect, so say for each input whether it pushes towards or against the prediction, and how strongly. State no probability and no number of the model, because the regulator judges the logic of the model and not its calibration.

When an audience is wrong

Two mistakes are easy to make, and both fail early, before any LLM call and before you pay for one. An unknown name. A string selects a built-in audience only. A custom audience is passed as an object.

Now call the LLM. explain_instance takes the audience as an object. It needs the global explanation of the model, computed once with describe_ebm. That is the slow step: one chain per feature, then a summary. Both buttons ask the LLM, and nothing runs before you press one.
